rows.description: A parent or mentor sees a proud student say yes to everything and praises the results. Praising output alone rewards overload, so noticing rest, limits and enjoyment matters just as much.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 23–26
related mind states: excitement, pride

rows.subtype: Stage 5: Body and mood sound the alarm [Actor]
rows.description: A young engineer gets headaches, stomach trouble, irritability at home and dread every Sunday night. Body and temper are sending a message that the schedule, not personal weakness, is the problem.
graph_context: next stage: Collapse or forced stop
this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22
related mind states: fear

rows.subtype: Stage 5: Body and mood sound the alarm [Observer]
rows.description: A colleague sees a once-cheerful teammate turn sharp and forgetful and start missing lunch. A quiet private check-in works better than remarks in the group, and pointing to a doctor beats saying just take a break.
graph_context: next stage: Collapse or forced stop
this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22
related mind states: joy

rows.description: The person breaks down, sleeps through a weekend, or cannot get out of bed for a Monday deadline. The crash feels like failure, but it is the body enforcing the rest that the mind refused.
graph_context: previous stage: Body and mood sound the alarm
next stage: Honest talk and boundaries
this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22

rows.description: The person tells a manager or family the truth about their load, drops or hands off tasks and protects sleep and meals. Speaking up early costs less than a breakdown, and good managers respond with adjustments, not blame.
graph_context: previous stage: Collapse or forced stop
next stage: Slow rebuilding
this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22

rows.description: Recovery takes weeks to months, with good and flat days. The person returns to work in smaller steps, restores what fed them such as walks, family and play, and stops measuring worth only by output.
graph_context: previous stage: Honest talk and boundaries
this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22

rows.description: A child announces they will practise cricket, drawing or the harmonium every day after watching someone admired. The motive is excitement, and a new habit is easy while excitement lasts.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: admiration, excitement

rows.description: A teenager keeps a study or fitness routine for two weeks and enjoys ticking the calendar. The streak becomes part of their identity, which helps, but it also makes one slip feel like a disaster.
graph_context: next stage: Novelty fades
this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: pride

rows.description: By week three the routine feels dull and results are slow. The mind bargains that skipping one day will not hurt, and the effort now depends on discipline rather than mood.
graph_context: previous stage: Early streak and pride
this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: hurt

rows.description: A trip, exam or illness breaks the routine for a few days. The person feels guilty, reasons that the streak is ruined anyway and drifts into stopping altogether. This all-or-nothing reading does the real damage.
graph_context: next stage: Shame and avoidance
this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 13–17, 23–26
related mind states: guilt
